What is overfitting?

Overfitting is when a model memorizes the training data instead of learning the pattern — like a student who memorized last year's answers and fails when the questions change. Quick check: would you rather have 90% on practice tests and 60% on the real exam, or 80% and 79%?

Why do we split data into train and test sets?

So the model is graded on questions it has never seen — otherwise it can just recite answers it memorized. Quick check: if your test set accidentally overlaps your train set, is a high score trustworthy?

What does a learning rate control?
How big each correction step is — too big and you overshoot the valley, too small and training takes forever. Quick check: if loss bounces around wildly, would you raise or lower it?

Explain precision vs recall.

Precision: of the alarms I raised, how many were real. Recall: of the real problems, how many did I catch — a smoke detector tuned for precision stays silent but misses fires; tuned for recall, it screams at toast. Quick check: for cancer screening, which would you prioritize?

What is an epoch?
One full pass over the training data — like reading the textbook once. Quick check: if the model improves for 3 epochs then gets worse, what's happening?

Why normalize input features?
So no feature dominates just because of its units — salary in rupees would drown age in years. Quick check: what happens to gradient steps when features are on wildly different scales?

What is a validation set for?
Choosing between models and settings — it's the mock exam you use to pick your study strategy, kept separate from the final exam. Quick check: why is tuning on the test set considered cheating?

What does batch size change?

How many examples the model grades before updating — small batches give noisier but more frequent feedback; large batches are steadier but need more memory. Quick check: with a tiny GPU, would you raise or lower batch size?
